claim: The receptome is a measure of interareal chemoarchitectural similarity derived from positron-emission tomography imaging studies of 19 different neurotransmitter transporters and receptors.
source: Here, we studied the organization of the receptome, a measure of interareal chemoarchitectural similarity, derived from positron-emission tomography imaging studies of 19 different neurotransmitter transporters and receptors.
evidence: The definition and methodology for the receptome is explicitly stated in the abstract and described in detail in the methods section.

claim: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction revealed three main spatial gradients of cortical chemoarchitectural similarity: a centro-temporal gradient, an occipito-frontal gradient, and a temporo-occipital gradient.
source: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction revealed three main spatial gradients of cortical chemoarchitectural similarity – a centro-temporal gradient, an occipito-frontal gradient, and a temporo-occipital gradient.
evidence: The three gradients are identified through diffusion map embedding analysis of the receptome data.

claim: In subcortical nuclei, chemoarchitectural similarity distinguished functional communities and delineated a striato-thalamic axis.
source: In subcortical nuclei, chemoarchitectural similarity distinguished functional communities and delineated a striato-thalamic axis.
evidence: This finding is supported by Leiden clustering and gradient decomposition analyses of subcortical structures.

claim: The cortical receptome shared key organizational traits with functional and structural brain anatomy.
source: Overall, the cortical receptome shared key organizational traits with functional and structural brain anatomy, with node-level correspondence to functional, microstructural, and diffusion MRI-based measures decreasing along a primary-to-transmodal axis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through correlation analyses between receptome gradients and gradients of functional connectivity, structural connectivity, and microstructural profile covariance.

claim: Node-level correspondence between the receptome and functional, microstructural, and diffusion MRI-based measures decreases along a primary-to-transmodal axis.
source: Overall, the cortical receptome shared key organizational traits with functional and structural brain anatomy, with node-level correspondence to functional, microstructural, and diffusion MRI-based measures decreasing along a primary-to-transmodal axis.
evidence: This is shown through coupling analyses that demonstrate decreasing correlation strength from idiotypic to heteromodal and paralimbic cortices.

claim: Relative to primary and paralimbic regions, unimodal and heteromodal regions showed higher receptomic diversification.
source: Relative to primary and paralimbic regions, unimodal and heteromodal regions showed higher receptomic diversification, possibly supporting functional flexibility.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modular stability analysis showing that heteromodal and unimodal cortices have more diverse chemoarchitectural landscapes.

claim: Higher receptomic diversification in unimodal and heteromodal regions possibly supports functional flexibility.
source: Relative to primary and paralimbic regions, unimodal and heteromodal regions showed higher receptomic diversification, possibly supporting functional flexibility.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed receptomic diversification pattern.

claim: Brain areas vary substantially in cellular composition.
source: Histological mapping studies found that brain areas vary substantially in cellular composition and established a link between cytoarchitectural and functional diversity (Brodmann, 1909; von Koskinas and Koskinas, 1925; Vogt and Vogt, 1919).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical histological mapping studies.

claim: There is a link between cytoarchitectural and functional diversity in the brain.
source: Histological mapping studies found that brain areas vary substantially in cellular composition and established a link between cytoarchitectural and functional diversity (Brodmann, 1909; von Koskinas and Koskinas, 1925; Vogt and Vogt, 1919).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical histological mapping studies.

claim: Neurotransmitter receptors show a heterogeneous distribution throughout the cortex.
source: Neurotransmitter receptors show a heterogeneous distribution throughout the cortex, closely related to both vertical (laminar) and horizontal cyto- and myeloarchitectural composition, as shown using postmortem autoradiographical receptor labeling (Eickhoff et al., 2007; Zilles and Amunts, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to autoradiography studies.

claim: Neurotransmitter receptor distribution is closely related to both vertical (laminar) and horizontal cyto- and myeloarchitectural composition.
source: Neurotransmitter receptors show a heterogeneous distribution throughout the cortex, closely related to both vertical (laminar) and horizontal cyto- and myeloarchitectural composition, as shown using postmortem autoradiographical receptor labeling (Eickhoff et al., 2007; Zilles and Amunts, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to autoradiography studies.

claim: Receptor distributions recapitulate histology-defined cortical areas.
source: Receptor distributions recapitulate histology-defined cortical areas, but also organize different cortical areas into neurochemical families and further subdivide homogeneous cytoarchitectural regions (Zilles and Amunts, 2009; Zilles and Palomero-Gallagher, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Receptor distributions organize different cortical areas into neurochemical families.
source: Receptor distributions recapitulate histology-defined cortical areas, but also organize different cortical areas into neurochemical families and further subdivide homogeneous cytoarchitectural regions (Zilles and Amunts, 2009; Zilles and Palomero-Gallagher, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Receptor distributions further subdivide homogeneous cytoarchitectural regions.
source: Receptor distributions recapitulate histology-defined cortical areas, but also organize different cortical areas into neurochemical families and further subdivide homogeneous cytoarchitectural regions (Zilles and Amunts, 2009; Zilles and Palomero-Gallagher, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Changes in localized brain function are reflected by changes in receptor distributions.
source: Changes in localized brain function are reflected by changes in receptor distributions, as demonstrated in the changes of multiple receptor densities at the border between primary (V1) and secondary (V2) visual cortex (Eickhoff et al., 2008; Zilles et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing receptor density changes at the V1/V2 border.

claim: Multiple receptor densities change at the border between primary (V1) and secondary (V2) visual cortex.
source: Changes in localized brain function are reflected by changes in receptor distributions, as demonstrated in the changes of multiple receptor densities at the border between primary (V1) and secondary (V2) visual cortex (Eickhoff et al., 2008; Zilles et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Brain areas sharing similar functionalities display similarities in the density profiles of multiple neurotransmitter receptor types.
source: Crucially, brain areas sharing similar functionalities also display similarities in the density profiles of multiple neurotransmitter receptor types, the so-called receptor 'fingerprint' (Zilles and Amunts, 2009; Zilles et al., 2004; Zilles et al., 2002; Morosan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on receptor fingerprints.

claim: Receptor fingerprints delineate sensory from association cortices.
source: For example, receptor fingerprints delineate sensory from association cortices (Dehaene et al., 2005) and provide a common molecular basis of areas involved in language comprehension (Zilles et al., 2015), strongly indicating receptor fingerprints as key features supporting functional specialization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dehaene et al., 2005.

claim: Receptor fingerprints provide a common molecular basis of areas involved in language comprehension.
source: For example, receptor fingerprints delineate sensory from association cortices (Dehaene et al., 2005) and provide a common molecular basis of areas involved in language comprehension (Zilles et al., 2015), strongly indicating receptor fingerprints as key features supporting functional specialization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zilles et al., 2015.

claim: Receptor fingerprints are key features supporting functional specialization.
source: For example, receptor fingerprints delineate sensory from association cortices (Dehaene et al., 2005) and provide a common molecular basis of areas involved in language comprehension (Zilles et al., 2015), strongly indicating receptor fingerprints as key features supporting functional specialization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited evidence about receptor fingerprints and functional organization.

claim: Brain regions in the same resting-state functional connectivity networks display increased chemoarchitectural similarities.
source: Importantly, they showed that brain regions in the same resting-state functional connectivity (FC) networks as well as structurally connected brain regions display increased chemoarchitectural similarities (Hansen et al., 2022), replicating structure–function relationships evident from autoradiography studies (Zilles and Amunts, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hansen et al., 2022.

claim: Structurally connected brain regions display increased chemoarchitectural similarities.
source: Importantly, they showed that brain regions in the same resting-state functional connectivity (FC) networks as well as structurally connected brain regions display increased chemoarchitectural similarities (Hansen et al., 2022), replicating structure–function relationships evident from autoradiography studies (Zilles and Amunts, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hansen et al., 2022.

claim: Alterations in NTRM expression and distribution patterns are linked to psychiatric diseases.
source: NTRMs are highly relevant in mental health care, as an extensive body of research links alterations in NTRM expression and distribution patterns to psychiatric diseases (Nautiyal and Hen, 2017; Seeman, 2013; Quah et al., 2020; Lydiard, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to research on NTRMs and psychiatric diseases.

claim: Most psychotropic drugs manipulate the brain's neurotransmission landscape.
source: Additionally, most psychotropic drugs manipulate the brain's neurotransmission landscape and are effective and reliable pillars in the treatment of psychiatric diseases (Cipriani et al., 2018; Huhn et al., 2019; Soomro et al., 2008; Geddes and Miklowitz, 2013), although their mechanisms of action are often incompletely understood.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to research on psychotropic drugs.

claim: Psychotropic drugs are effective and reliable pillars in the treatment of psychiatric diseases.
source: Additionally, most psychotropic drugs manipulate the brain's neurotransmission landscape and are effective and reliable pillars in the treatment of psychiatric diseases (Cipriani et al., 2018; Huhn et al., 2019; Soomro et al., 2008; Geddes and Miklowitz, 2013), although their mechanisms of action are often incompletely understood.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to research on psychotropic drugs.

claim: The mechanisms of action of psychotropic drugs are often incompletely understood.
source: Additionally, most psychotropic drugs manipulate the brain's neurotransmission landscape and are effective and reliable pillars in the treatment of psychiatric diseases (Cipriani et al., 2018; Huhn et al., 2019; Soomro et al., 2008; Geddes and Miklowitz, 2013), although their mechanisms of action are often incompletely understood.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the field.

claim: Clinical phenotypes are associated with alterations in multiple neurotransmitter systems.
source: Complementary, clinical phenotypes are associated with alterations in multiple neurotransmitter systems (Moncrieff et al., 2022; Kaltenboeck and Harmer, 2018; Kesby et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to research on clinical phenotypes and neurotransmitter systems.

claim: Cortical disparities between functional and structural connectivity could be partly explained by subcortical ascending neuromodulatory projections.
source: Since cortical disparities between functional and structural connectivity could be partly explained by subcortical ascending neuromodulatory projections (Bell and Shine, 2016; Shine, 2019), a clearer understanding of subcortical chemoarchitecture and its relationship to cortical chemoarchitecture could provide a novel perspective on whole-brain structure–function relationships (Forstmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bell and Shine, 2016 and Shine, 2019.

claim: The first receptome gradient (RC G1) described an axis stretching between somato-motor regions and inferior temporal and occipital lobe.
source: The first receptome gradient (RC G1) described an axis stretching between somato-motor regions and inferior temporal and occipital lobe.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the results text.

claim: The second receptome gradient (RC G2) spanned between a temporo-occipital and a frontal anchor.
source: The second receptome gradient (RC G2) spanned between a temporo-occipital and a frontal anchor.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the results text.

claim: The third receptome gradient (RC G3) was differentiated between the occipital cortex and the temporal lobe.
source: Finally, the third receptome gradient (RC G3) was differentiated between the occipital cortex and the temporal lobe (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the results text.

claim: RC G1 was primarily driven by the anticorrelation between distributions of 5-HTT, 5-HT4, 5-HT2a, and GABAa with the distributions of VAChT, H3, NAT, and Α4Β2.
source: RC G1 was primarily driven by the anticorrelation between distributions of 5-HTT, 5-HT4, 5-HT2a, and GABAa with the distributions of VAChT, H3, NAT, and Α4Β2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and described in the results text.

claim: RC G2 separated 5-HTT, DAT, NMDA, D1, and GABA distributions from α4β2, 5-HT1b, CB1, H3, and MU.
source: RC G2 separated 5-HTT, DAT, NMDA, D1, and GABA distributions from α4β2, 5-HT1b, CB1, H3, and MU.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and described in the results text.

claim: RC G3 showed significant negative correlations to GABAa distributions and significant positive correlations to D1, 5-HT1a, CB1, MU, 5-HT4, and VAChT.
source: RC G3 showed significant negative correlations to GABAa distributions and significant positive correlations to D1, 5-HT1a, CB1, MU, 5-HT4, and VAChT.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and described in the results text.

claim: Subcortical nuclei were shown to be largely separate from cortical structures in their chemoarchitectural composition, with the exception of amygdala.
source: Subcortical nuclei were shown to be largely separate from cortical structures, with the exception of amygdala.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A through multidimensional scaling projection.

claim: Subcortical chemoarchitecture was largely symmetrical between hemispheres.
source: Subcortical chemoarchitecture was largely symmetrical between hemispheres, as indicated by the immediate clustering of structures with their counterpart from the other hemisphere.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A through hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: The main hierarchical branch separated putamen, accumbens nucleus, caudate nucleus (the striatum), and pallidum from amygdala and thalamus.
source: The main hierarchical branch separated putamen, accumbens nucleus, caudate nucleus (the striatum), and pallidum from amygdala and thalamus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A through hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: Thalamus and striatum had considerable differences in NTRM co-expression patterns.
source: Thalamus and striatum had considerable differences in NTRM co-expression patterns. α4β2, NAT, 5-HTT, and NMDA showed strong co-expression in thalamus but not in striatum, while D1, D2, DAT, 5-HT4, 5-HT6, M1, and VAChT were strongly co-expressed in striatum, but not in thalamus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A through hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: The first subcortical receptome gradient (sRC G1) explained 23% of relative variance.
source: The first subcortical receptome gradient (sRC G1), explaining 23% of relative variance, was anchored between the striatum and the thalamus (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and described in the results text.

claim: The first subcortical receptome gradient (sRC G1) was anchored between the striatum and the thalamus.
source: The first subcortical receptome gradient (sRC G1), explaining 23% of relative variance, was anchored between the striatum and the thalamus (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and described in the results text.

claim: Proximity of structures was not a major determinant of sRC G1 values.
source: Note that proximity of structures was not a major determinant of sRC G1 values, demonstrated by voxels of the caudate nucleus and thalamus that were proximal to each other but showed diverging sRC G1 values.
evidence: This observation is made from the spatial distribution of gradient values shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The first subcortical receptome gradient showed significant positive correlations to NAT, α4β2, and 5-HT2a densities.
source: The first subcortical receptome gradient showed significant positive correlations to NAT, α4β2, and 5-HT2a densities, and significant negative correlations to 5-HT6, D1, M1, 5-HT4, D2, DAT, VAChT, H3, and mGluR5 distributions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and described in the results text.

claim: The first subcortical receptome gradient showed significant negative correlations to 5-HT6, D1, M1, 5-HT4, D2, DAT, VAChT, H3, and mGluR5 distributions.
source: The first subcortical receptome gradient showed significant positive correlations to NAT, α4β2, and 5-HT2a densities, and significant negative correlations to 5-HT6, D1, M1, 5-HT4, D2, DAT, VAChT, H3, and mGluR5 distributions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and described in the results text.

claim: RC G1 showed strong positive correlations with meta-analytical topics of sensory-motor function (topics 2, 17, and 32) and control (topics 16 and 20).
source: RC G1 showed strong positive correlations with meta-analytical topics of sensory-motor function (topics 2, 17, and 32) and control (topics 16 and 20).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through Neurosynth meta-analytic decoding.

claim: RC G1 showed strongest negative correlations to topics capturing facial and emotion recognition (topic 40) and categorizing and abstract functions (topic 38).
source: Its strongest negative correlations were to topics capturing facial and emotion recognition (topic 40) as well as categorizing and abstract functions (topic 38).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through Neurosynth meta-analytic decoding.

claim: RC G2 displayed positive correlations to topics of control (topics 16, 20, and 48) and memory (topic 9).
source: RC G2 displayed positive correlations to topics of control (topics 16, 20, and 48) and memory (topic 9), differentiating them from topics of facial and emotion recognition (topic 40) and categorizing and abstract functions (topic 38), with which it showed negative correlations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through Neurosynth meta-analytic decoding.

claim: RC G2 showed negative correlations to topics of facial and emotion recognition (topic 40) and categorizing and abstract functions (topic 38).
source: RC G2 displayed positive correlations to topics of control (topics 16, 20, and 48) and memory (topic 9), differentiating them from topics of facial and emotion recognition (topic 40) and categorizing and abstract functions (topic 38), with which it showed negative correlations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through Neurosynth meta-analytic decoding.

claim: RC G3 showed positive correlations to topics related to language and speech (topics 6 and 46).
source: Lastly, RC G3 showed positive correlations of note to topics related to language and speech (topics 6 and 46) compared to negative correlations to topics of attention and task performance (topics 15 and 47), memory (topic 9), and mental imagery (topic 41).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through Neurosynth meta-analytic decoding.

claim: RC G3 showed negative correlations to topics of attention and task performance (topics 15 and 47), memory (topic 9), and mental imagery (topic 41).
source: Lastly, RC G3 showed positive correlations of note to topics related to language and speech (topics 6 and 46) compared to negative correlations to topics of attention and task performance (topics 15 and 47), memory (topic 9), and mental imagery (topic 41).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through Neurosynth meta-analytic decoding.

claim: RC G1 showed positive correlations to the cortical thickness profile of OCD.
source: RC G1 showed positive correlations to the cortical thickness profile of OCD, while RC G2 had negative correlations to cortical thickness alterations in BPD.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C through correlation with ENIGMA disease maps.

claim: RC G2 had negative correlations to cortical thickness alterations in BPD.
source: RC G1 showed positive correlations to the cortical thickness profile of OCD, while RC G2 had negative correlations to cortical thickness alterations in BPD.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C through correlation with ENIGMA disease maps.

claim: RC G3 did not show significant associations with cortical disease profiles.
source: RC G3 did not show significant associations with cortical disease profiles. (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C through correlation with ENIGMA disease maps.

claim: RC G1 showed alignment to the somato-motor network.
source: RC G1 showed alignment to the somato-motor network that forms its positive anchor.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 through variogram matching analysis.

claim: RC G2 was aligned to default mode and control networks and the visual network.
source: RC G2 was aligned to default mode and control networks, which are located in the positively anchoring regions, and the visual network, which is located on the opposite side of the gradient.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 through variogram matching analysis.

claim: RC G3 was aligned with limbic and visual networks.
source: Lastly, RC G3 was aligned with limbic and visual networks, which are located at opposite poles of the gradient.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 through variogram matching analysis.

claim: RC G1 showed strongest overlaps to SC G1 and FC G1.
source: RC G1 showed strongest overlaps to SC G1 and FC G1 as these gradients shared either anterior-posterior or visual-to-somatomotor trajectories (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through correlation analysis between gradient modalities.

claim: RC G1 showed weaker correlations with BB G1 and MPC G1.
source: Additional weaker correlations were observed with BB G1 and MPC G1, which represent the main axes of cortical cytoarchitectural similarity (Paquola et al., 2019), and FC G2, which separates unimodal from association cortices (Margulies et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through correlation analysis between gradient modalities.

claim: RC G2 correlated significantly to SC G1 and FC G1.
source: Similar to the first receptome gradient, RC G2 correlated significantly to SC G1 and FC G1, while separating visuo-limbic from control networks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through correlation analysis between gradient modalities.

claim: RC G3 showed the strongest correlations to SC G2.
source: RC G3 showed the strongest correlations to SC G2, which separated occipital from temporal cortex.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through correlation analysis between gradient modalities.

claim: RC G3 showed significant correlations with FC G1, MPC G1, and BB G1.
source: Further significant correlations existed with FC G1, MPC G1, and BB G1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through correlation analysis between gradient modalities.

claim: Coupling strength of the receptome to SC, FC, and MPC decreased along a sensory-fugal gradient of laminar differentiation.
source: Generally, coupling strength of the receptome to the other measures decreased along a sensory-fugal gradient of laminar differentiation, an influential theoretical framework that attributes cognitive processing complexity to cortical areas using cytoarchitectural classes (Mesulam, 1998).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B through row-wise correlation analysis and is referenced to the Mesulam framework.

claim: Average coupling strength across cytoarchitectural classes was significantly different across all metrics.
source: Average coupling strength across cytoarchitectural classes was significantly different across all metrics.
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical testing (Kruskal-Wallis test) of coupling strengths across cytoarchitectural classes.

claim: RC-SC decoupling along the sensory-fugal gradient was driven by significantly stronger coupling in idiotypic relative to heteromodal and paralimbic cortices.
source: RC-SC decoupling along the sensory-fugal gradient (Kruskal–Wallis' h = 24.43, p<0.001) was driven by significantly stronger coupling in idiotypic relative to heteromodal and paralimbic cortices (post hoc Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction p<0.001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and supported by statistical testing.

claim: RC-FC coupling strengths in idiotypic cortices were significantly increased relative to unimodal, heteromodal, and paralimbic cortices.
source: RC-FC coupling strengths in idiotypic cortices were significantly increased relative to unimodal, heteromodal, and paralimbic cortices (h = 16.68, p<0.001; Dunn's test p<0.02).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and supported by statistical testing.

claim: RC-MPC decoupling across cytoarchitectural classes was primarily reflected by decreased coupling in heteromodal versus idiotypic regions.
source: Last, RC-MPC decoupling across cytoarchitectural classes (h = 9.16, p<0.05) was primarily reflected by decreased coupling in heteromodal versus idiotypic regions (Dunn's test p<0.02).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and supported by statistical testing.

claim: New receptomic communities primarily formed in the frontal cortex when sampling the resolution parameter space.
source: We observed that new communities primarily formed in the frontal cortex when sampling the resolution parameter space, indicating more unique NTRM fingerprints in the frontal cortex.
evidence: This observation is made from Leiden clustering analysis across different resolution parameters.

claim: Paralimbic cortices exhibited modular stability similar to idiotypic cortices.
source: Overall, paralimbic cortices exhibited modular stability similar to idiotypic cortices, while heteromodal and unimodal regions were less stable (Figure 4D), suggesting that idiotypic and paralimbic cortices contain a more homogeneous receptomic profile, while heteromodal and unimodal cortices have a more diverse chemoarchitectural landscape.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D through modular stability analysis.

claim: Heteromodal and unimodal regions were less stable in modular stability compared to idiotypic and paralimbic cortices.
source: Overall, paralimbic cortices exhibited modular stability similar to idiotypic cortices, while heteromodal and unimodal regions were less stable (Figure 4D), suggesting that idiotypic and paralimbic cortices contain a more homogeneous receptomic profile, while heteromodal and unimodal cortices have a more diverse chemoarchitectural landscape.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D through modular stability analysis.

claim: Idiotypic and paralimbic cortices contain a more homogeneous receptomic profile.
source: Overall, paralimbic cortices exhibited modular stability similar to idiotypic cortices, while heteromodal and unimodal regions were less stable (Figure 4D), suggesting that idiotypic and paralimbic cortices contain a more homogeneous receptomic profile, while heteromodal and unimodal cortices have a more diverse chemoarchitectural landscape.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modular stability analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Heteromodal and unimodal cortices have a more diverse chemoarchitectural landscape.
source: Overall, paralimbic cortices exhibited modular stability similar to idiotypic cortices, while heteromodal and unimodal regions were less stable (Figure 4D), suggesting that idiotypic and paralimbic cortices contain a more homogeneous receptomic profile, while heteromodal and unimodal cortices have a more diverse chemoarchitectural landscape.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modular stability analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Receptome gradients showed good replicability across parcellations.
source: Receptome gradients showed good replicability across parcellations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), although an increase in parcellation granularity shifted one extreme in RC G1 and RC G2 toward the temporal poles.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 through replication analysis across different parcellation granularities.

claim: An increase in parcellation granularity shifted one extreme in RC G1 and RC G2 toward the temporal poles.
source: Receptome gradients showed good replicability across parcellations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), although an increase in parcellation granularity shifted one extreme in RC G1 and RC G2 toward the temporal poles.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 through replication analysis across different parcellation granularities.

claim: For granularities of 200 and 400 parcels, there is a component ranking switch between RC G1 and RC G2.
source: Notably, for granularities of 200 and 400 parcels, there is a component ranking switch meaning that the pattern captured by RC G1 in the main results is captured by RC G2 in the replication, and vice versa.
evidence: This observation is made from the replication analysis across different parcellation granularities.

claim: Diffusion embedding-derived gradients showed high correspondence to axes derived by linear dimensionality reduction techniques.
source: Diffusion embedding-derived gradients showed high correspondence to axes derived by linear dimensionality reduction techniques (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A through comparison with PCA-derived components.

claim: The first 11 components explained significantly more variance compared to gradients decomposed from receptomes generated from randomized NTRM density maps.
source: The first 11 components explained significantly more variance compared to gradients decomposed from receptomes generated from randomized NTRM density maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B through null model comparison.

claim: The first three receptome gradients explained 15, 14, and 13% of relative variance, respectively.
source: We chose to focus on the first three gradients, which explained 15, 14, and 13% of relative variance, respectively, due to a marked drop in variance explained after these three components (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A in the variance explained plot.

claim: Receptomic clustering exhibited high stability across the resolution parameter sample space.
source: Subcortical receptome clustering exhibited high stability across the resolution parameter sample space (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A through Leiden clustering analysis.

claim: Receptomic clustering discerned three dominant communities: one mainly capturing striatal structures and pallidal globe, one mainly capturing the thalamus, and one mainly capturing the amygdala.
source: Receptomic clustering discerned three dominant communities, the first mainly capturing the striatal structures (putamen, caudate, NAc) and the pallidal globe, the second mainly capturing the thalamus, and the third mainly capturing the amygdala (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A through Leiden clustering analysis.

claim: The second subcortical gradient explained 17.5% of relative variance.
source: The second gradient, explaining 17.5% of relative variance, and third gradient, explaining 12% of relative variance, described ventral-dorsal and medial-lateral trajectories, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 through gradient decomposition analysis.

claim: The third subcortical gradient explained 12% of relative variance.
source: The second gradient, explaining 17.5% of relative variance, and third gradient, explaining 12% of relative variance, described ventral-dorsal and medial-lateral trajectories, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 through gradient decomposition analysis.

claim: The second subcortical gradient described a ventral-dorsal trajectory.
source: The second gradient, explaining 17.5% of relative variance, and third gradient, explaining 12% of relative variance, described ventral-dorsal and medial-lateral trajectories, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 through gradient decomposition analysis.

claim: The third subcortical gradient described a medial-lateral trajectory.
source: The second gradient, explaining 17.5% of relative variance, and third gradient, explaining 12% of relative variance, described ventral-dorsal and medial-lateral trajectories, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 through gradient decomposition analysis.

claim: The first and second cortical gradients correlated significantly with all subcortico-cortical receptome gradients.
source: The first and second cortical gradients correlated significantly with all subcortico-cortical receptome gradients, while the third cortical gradient only correlated significantly to the third subcortico-cortical gradient (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D through correlation analysis.

claim: The third cortical gradient only correlated significantly to the third subcortico-cortical gradient.
source: The first and second cortical gradients correlated significantly with all subcortico-cortical receptome gradients, while the third cortical gradient only correlated significantly to the third subcortico-cortical gradient (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D through correlation analysis.

claim: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) target 5-HTT and are the preferred pharmacological intervention to treat OCD.
source: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) target 5-HTT and are the preferred pharmacological intervention to treat OCD (Soomro et al., 2008; Lissemore et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on OCD treatment.

claim: 5-HT2a and 5-HTT variants have been identified as risk factors for the development of OCD.
source: Genetically, 5-HT2a and 5-HTT variants have been identified as risk factors for the development of OCD (Taylor, 2013), and OCD patients showed aberrant peripheral 5-HTT and 5-HT2a functionality (Delorme et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies of OCD.

claim: OCD patients showed aberrant peripheral 5-HTT and 5-HT2a functionality.
source: Genetically, 5-HT2a and 5-HTT variants have been identified as risk factors for the development of OCD (Taylor, 2013), and OCD patients showed aberrant peripheral 5-HTT and 5-HT2a functionality (Delorme et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Delorme et al., 2005.

claim: There is emerging evidence that GABA signaling abnormalities are related to the development of OCD.
source: In addition, there is emerging evidence that GABA signaling abnormalities are related to the development of OCD (Pauls et al., 2014), although conclusive evidence is lacking.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pauls et al., 2014, but noted as not conclusive.

claim: 5-HTT, DAT, and NMDA have been implicated in genesis and treatment of BPD.
source: Moreover, it associated cortical morphological alterations in BPD with features of NTRM fingerprints, where 5-HTT, DAT, and NMDA co-expression is of note. These NTRM have been implicated in genesis and treatment of BPD (Ghasemi et al., 2014; Ashok et al., 2017; Pinsonneault et al., 2011; Rao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to research on BPD and neurotransmitter systems.

claim: Visual and limbic cortices are relevant anchors in cortical chemoarchitectural similarity axes.
source: Gradient-based analysis indicated that visual and limbic cortices are relevant anchors in cortical chemoarchitectural similarity axes as they are polar at either one (RC G1 and G2) or both anchors of a gradient (RC G3).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gradient decomposition results showing visual and limbic cortices at gradient extremes.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of average NTRM densities separated both the visual and limbic network from other functional networks.
source: Hierarchical clustering of average NTRM densities separated both the visual and limbic network from other functional networks, mirroring clustering results obtained via autoradiography (Zilles and Palomero-Gallagher, 2017), and indicating more homogeneous chemoarchitectural compositions in these regions that, importantly, show little overlap between them.
evidence: This is shown through hierarchical clustering analysis and compared to autoradiography results.

claim: Visual and limbic networks have more homogeneous chemoarchitectural compositions that show little overlap between them.
source: Hierarchical clustering of average NTRM densities separated both the visual and limbic network from other functional networks, mirroring clustering results obtained via autoradiography (Zilles and Palomero-Gallagher, 2017), and indicating more homogeneous chemoarchitectural compositions in these regions that, importantly, show little overlap between them.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the hierarchical clustering results.

claim: Receptor similarity is organized in a fashion that combines organizational principles of cytoarchitectural, structural, and functional differentiation.
source: Summarizing the interrelationships of receptome gradients and brain structure and function, our results suggest that receptor similarity is organized in a fashion that combines organizational principles of cytoarchitectural, structural, and functional differentiation, although interrelationships to structural and functional connectivity and cytoarchitectural variation present themselves differently across parcellation granularities.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the multiple correlation analyses between receptome gradients and other brain organizational measures.

claim: Structural and functional connectivity is more closely linked in unimodal cortices and exhibits gradual decoupling toward transmodal cortices.
source: Previous work showed that structural and functional connectivity is more closely linked in unimodal cortices and exhibits gradual decoupling toward transmodal cortices, a phenomenon that is hypothesized to be instrumental for human flexible cognition (Preti and Van De Ville, 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Valk et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on structure-function coupling.

claim: Structure-function decoupling toward transmodal cortices is hypothesized to be instrumental for human flexible cognition.
source: Previous work showed that structural and functional connectivity is more closely linked in unimodal cortices and exhibits gradual decoupling toward transmodal cortices, a phenomenon that is hypothesized to be instrumental for human flexible cognition (Preti and Van De Ville, 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Valk et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a hypothesis cited from previous research.

claim: Diversification of NTRM fingerprints may be important to enable flexible cognitive functions.
source: Replicating this observation for chemoarchitectural similarity suggests that diversification of NTRM fingerprints may be equally important to enable flexible cognitive functions (Suárez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the observed pattern of receptomic diversification and cited theoretical framework.

claim: Associative areas show high segregation into subareas based on their receptor architecture.
source: This is consistent with associative areas showing high segregation into subareas based on their receptor architecture (Amunts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Amunts et al., 2010.

claim: High receptomic diversity might be a disease vulnerability factor.
source: High receptomic diversity might be a disease vulnerability factor as recent work has shown that cortical thickness alterations across different diseases are most pronounced in heteromodal cortices (Hettwer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed receptomic diversity pattern and cited research on disease-related cortical alterations.

claim: Cortical thickness alterations across different diseases are most pronounced in heteromodal cortices.
source: High receptomic diversity might be a disease vulnerability factor as recent work has shown that cortical thickness alterations across different diseases are most pronounced in heteromodal cortices (Hettwer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hettwer et al., 2022.

claim: Primary regions show a lesser degree of interindividual neuroanatomical variability compared to heteromodal regions.
source: However, it has to be noted that primary regions show a lesser degree of interindividual neuroanatomical variability compared to heteromodal regions, which could be a possible methodological confound influencing our finding of sensory-to-fugal architectural decoupling (Mueller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mueller et al., 2013 and noted as a potential confound.

claim: Heteromodal regions show decreased heritability and cross-species similarity compared to paralimbic regions.
source: Additionally, recent work has indicated a differentiation between heteromodal and paralimbic regions, where the former show decreased heritability and cross-species similarity (Valk et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Valk et al., 2022.

claim: Basal ganglia are implicated in motor functions and complex signal integration.
source: Striatum and pallidal globe constitute the basal ganglia, which, together with the thalamus, form the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic loop. Here, basal ganglia are implicated in motor functions and complex signal integration, while the thalamus orchestrates the communication between large-scale cortical networks (Bell and Shine, 2016; Hwang et al., 2017; Lanciego et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on basal ganglia function.

claim: The thalamus orchestrates the communication between large-scale cortical networks.
source: Striatum and pallidal globe constitute the basal ganglia, which, together with the thalamus, form the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic loop. Here, basal ganglia are implicated in motor functions and complex signal integration, while the thalamus orchestrates the communication between large-scale cortical networks (Bell and Shine, 2016; Hwang et al., 2017; Lanciego et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on thalamic function.

claim: 5-HTT and α4β2 distributions in the cortex are prominently anticorrelated.
source: For example, 5-HTT and α4β2 distributions in the cortex are prominently anticorrelated but show similar distributions in subcortial nuclei.
evidence: This is observed from the correlation analyses of NTRM distributions with gradients in cortex and subcortex.

claim: 5-HTT and α4β2 show similar distributions in subcortical nuclei.
source: For example, 5-HTT and α4β2 distributions in the cortex are prominently anticorrelated but show similar distributions in subcortial nuclei.
evidence: This is observed from the correlation analyses of NTRM distributions with gradients in cortex and subcortex.

claim: The α2 noradrenaline receptor is an important drug target in the central nervous system.
source: Important molecules such as the α2 noradrenaline receptor, which is an important drug target in the central nervous system (Smith and Elliott, 2001; Alam et al., 2013), are missing from our dataset.
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on α2 noradrenaline receptor as a drug target.

claim: D1 and D2 signaling influence NMDA signaling through cAMP-mediated posttranslational modification of the receptor.
source: For example, D1 and D2 signaling influence NMDA signaling through cAMP-mediated posttranslational modification of the receptor, directly acting upon its neuromodulatory potential (Neve et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Neve et al., 2004.

claim: The neuromodulatory potency of 5-HTT depends on the postsynaptic availability of serotonin receptors.
source: Similarly, neuromodulation through presynaptic transporters is conjunct with receptor expression. For example, the neuromodulatory potency of 5-HTT depends on the postsynaptic availability of serotonin receptors, which would mediate the effect an inhibition of these molecules via a drug, such as Fluoxetine.
evidence: This is stated as an example of the interdependence between transporters and receptors in neuromodulation.

claim: The thalamus consists of more than 60 nuclei with distinct cellular composition and diverging functionality.
source: For example, the thalamus consists of more than 60 nuclei with distinct cellular composition and diverging functionality (Fama and Sullivan, 2015), important properties we cannot pick up on.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fama and Sullivan, 2015.

claim: The PET dataset used contains over 1200 subjects.
source: To assess cortical chemoarchitecture, we leveraged a large publicly available dataset of PET-derived NTRM densities, containing 19 different NTRM from a total of over 1200 subjects (Hansen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the dataset used.

claim: The receptor maps were parcellated into 100 parcels according to the Schaefer atlas.
source: After parcellating the receptor maps into 100 parcels according to the Schaefer atlas (Schaefer et al., 2018), we calculated a Spearman rank correlation matrix of parcel-level NTRM densities, the receptome.
evidence: This is stated as part of the methodology.

claim: The receptome represents node-level interregional similarities in NTRM fingerprints.
source: The receptome represents node-level interregional similarities in NTRM fingerprints.
evidence: This is stated as a definition of the receptome.

claim: The accuracy and validity of receptor density as derived from the PET images have been confirmed using autoradiography data.
source: The accuracy and validity of receptor density as derived from the PET images have been confirmed using autoradiography data, and the mean age of participants was shown to have negligible influence on tracer density values (Hansen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hansen et al., 2022.

claim: The mean age of participants was shown to have negligible influence on tracer density values.
source: The accuracy and validity of receptor density as derived from the PET images have been confirmed using autoradiography data, and the mean age of participants was shown to have negligible influence on tracer density values (Hansen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hansen et al., 2022.

claim: The MICA-MICs dataset was acquired from 50 healthy young adults with no prior history of neurological or mental illnesses.
source: MRI data was acquired at the Brain Imaging Centre of the Montreal Neurological Institute and Hospital using a 3T Siemens Magnetom Prisma-Fit equipped with a 64-channel head coil from 50 healthy young adults with no prior history of neurological or mental illnesses (23 women; 29.54 ± 5.62 y).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the dataset used for SC, FC, and MPC analyses.

claim: Distance-dependent thresholding was applied to account for the over-representation of short-range and under-representation of long-range connections in non-thresholded group-consensus SC matrices.
source: Afterward, we applied distance-dependent thresholding to account for the over-representation of short-range and under-representation of long-range connections in non-thresholded group-consensus SC matrices (Betzel et al., 2019), and the resulting thresholded matrix was used in subsequent analyses.
evidence: This is stated as part of the methodology and supported by a citation to Betzel et al., 2019.
